Security forces gained control of the first two floors and eventually made their way to the top, finally taking control of it and arresting the gunmen Monday afternoon. Television pictures showed security forces firing into the air from the roof of the building after the firefight. "The operation is over. Four terrorists were killed and three arrested," Interior Ministry Secretary Kamal Shah told Reuters. Malik and Abbas confirmed the figures. Abbas added some of the dead militants blew themselves up. The gang of seven gunmen stormed the academy in the Manawan area of the eastern Pakistani city, said Malik. Abbas had previously said 30 people were killed. Mehsud is also accused of plotting the assassination of former PM Benazir Bhutto. At least 78 people were wounded in the attack, authorities said. Lahore is the same city where gunmen opened fire March 10 on a bus carrying members of the Sri Lankan national cricket team on their way to a stadium for a match. The well-coordinated attack wounded at least eight members of the team and killed a driver and six Pakistani police officers. In Monday's incident, the attackers hurled grenades, then stormed the compound and opened fire while officers were taking part in their morning drill. The attackers, some in police uniforms, took dozens of officers hostage, said Asim Rizwan, spokesman for governor of Punjab -- the province where Lahore is located. Paramilitary forces and the army descended on the scene. Every few minutes, the gunmen detonated explosives or fired on reporters and police personnel outside, sending them scurrying for cover. Angry onlookers pumped their fists in the air and cheered as police led away a suspect they had captured. He had on him a grenade and a knife, officials told CNN. CNN's Reza Sayah contributed to this report.

**Siege in Lahore: How Pakistani Forces Overcame a Deadly Police Academy Assault**

In a brazen display of urban terror, heavily armed militants launched a coordinated assault on the Manawan Police Training Center on the outskirts of Lahore, Pakistan. What began as a chaotic morning routine for hundreds of unarmed recruits rapidly descended into a desperate, high-stakes battle. Following an intense eight-hour counter-operation led by elite security forces, the siege concluded with the complex secured, but not before leaving a grim trail of casualties and deepening the nation's growing security crisis.

### The Attack Begins

The morning assault was meticulously planned to inflict maximum chaos. Dressed in civilian clothing and, in some cases, security uniforms, a cell of seven militants breached the perimeter of the sprawling, 80-acre training facility while hundreds of recruits were participating in morning parade drills. 

Surprising the guards at the main gate, the attackers opened fire with assault rifles and detonated hand grenades, creating a wall of smoke and noise. Panic surged through the parade ground as unarmed recruits scrambled for cover under a hail of automatic gunfire. Taking advantage of the initial confusion, the insurgents pushed deep into the compound, barricading themselves inside the main administrative and residential buildings. Positioned on the upper floors and rooftop, the gunmen established defensive firing positions, effectively holding the compound hostage and pinning down surviving officers inside.

### The Eight-Hour Counter-Operation

As news of the attack broke, Pakistani security forces—including military commandos from the Special Services Group (SSG), the paramilitary Rangers, and Elite Police units—converged on the facility, establishing a tight perimeter. Army helicopters hovered overhead, providing aerial intelligence, while snipers took up positions on surrounding structures.

What followed was a methodical, high-risk counter-operation that lasted eight grueling hours. With the militants dug into fortified positions inside the multi-story buildings, security forces had to execute a floor-by-floor, room-by-room clearance. 

Advancing behind armored shields under heavy fire, commandos systematically moved through the corridors. Distant explosions and sustained bursts of gunfire echoed across the complex as team members cleared each room, wary of potential booby traps or suicide vests. Floor by floor, the assault teams squeezed the insurgents into smaller pockets of resistance. By late afternoon, snipers eliminated key gunmen on the roof, allowing assault teams to make a final push into the remaining strongholds.

### Casualties and the Toll

By the time the final firing ceased and the building was declared secure, the human toll of the assault was laid bare. Eight security personnel—mostly young police recruits and brave early responders—were killed in the opening salvos and subsequent fighting. Another 78 individuals suffered injuries ranging from gunshot wounds to shrapnel damage, flooding local Lahore hospitals that were placed on emergency readiness.

All seven attackers were neutralized by the end of the operation. Four were killed in firefights with security forces or detonated their explosive vests to avoid capture, while three were taken into custody alive by commandos—providing intelligence agencies with critical assets for immediate interrogation.

### The Prime Suspect and Political Fallout

As forensic teams swept the bullet-riddled, blood-stained facility, Pakistani authorities quickly turned their attention to the architects of the raid. High-level security officials named Baitullah Mehsud, the leader of the Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), as the prime suspect behind the operation. 

Mehsud, operating out of the lawless tribal region of Waziristan, had increasingly targeted state infrastructure, military installations, and police apparatus in an effort to destabilize the government. The Lahore attack signaled a terrifying shift in strategy: moving the front lines of the insurgency from the rugged western borderlands directly into the heart of Pakistan’s cultural capital.

The siege highlighted both the extreme vulnerability of soft state targets and the growing resolve of Pakistan's elite tactical units under pressure. In the aftermath of the assault, the government vowed to intensify military operations against Mehsud’s network in the tribal areas, marking the Lahore academy attack as a key tipping point in the nation's ongoing struggle against domestic violent extremism.

The attack on the Manawan Police Academy, located near the Indian border, marked the second major terrorist strike in Lahore in less than a month, underscoring the expanding reach of militant networks from Pakistan’s volatile tribal regions into its urban heartland.

According to military and hospital sources, the dead included eight police recruits, two civilians, and at least two of the attackers. More than 90 police cadets and instructors were rushed to local facilities, including Mayo Hospital, many suffering from gunshot wounds and shrapnel injuries from hand grenades.

### A Dawn Ambush

The attack began at approximately 7:30 a.m. local time during the academy's morning parade. Witnesses said a group of 10 to 12 gunmen—dressed in civilian clothes and tactical vests, armed with assault rifles, hand grenades, and rockets—scaled the perimeter walls and threw explosives over the compound gates.

"We were standing in formation on the parade ground when explosions shattered the morning," said one surviving recruit, his uniform stained with blood. "Grenades were falling everywhere, and then they opened fire from multiple angles. It was complete chaos."

The attackers quickly took control of the main administration building and held dozens of recruits hostage, using rooftops to fire on responding security forces. 

The standoff triggered a massive counter-operation involving the army's Elite Commando units, the paramilitary Rangers, and local police. Armed with snipers and supported by military helicopters hovering overhead, security personnel launched a room-by-room sweep of the facility. The siege ended mid-afternoon after a fiery final assault by commandos.

### Official Responses: "An Attack on Pakistan's Sovereignty"

Top government and military officials framed the assault as part of an existential conflict facing the nation.

Rehman Malik, the chief advisor to the Prime Minister on Internal Affairs, stated that the attack was a calculated attempt to destabilize the country's law enforcement apparatus. Speaking to reporters in Islamabad, Malik revealed that at least one suspect had been captured alive near the compound carrying hand grenades and a fake identification card.

"This is an attack on the sovereignty of Pakistan," Malik said. "The terrorists are trying to destroy the peace of our country. They are organized, well-trained, and ruthless, but we will hunt them down. Initial interrogations of the captured suspect point toward elements operating from the tribal areas."

Malik added that the tactics employed mirrored previous high-profile regional assaults, suggesting a coordinated effort by extremist groups linked to the Pakistani Taliban (TTP).

Addressing the media following the resolution of the operation, chief military spokesman Maj. Gen. Athar Abbas confirmed that the facility had been successfully cleared by military and paramilitary forces.

"The academy has been completely secured," Gen. Abbas said. "During the tactical phase of the operation, four terrorists were killed by our forces, and three were captured alive. Our commandos acted with extreme caution to minimize casualties among the trapped recruits."

Gen. Abbas emphasized that intelligence agencies were working to identify the foreign and domestic linkages of the attackers, noting that a significant stash of unused explosives, suicide vests, and communication gear was recovered from the scene.

### Growing Wave of Regional Violence

The assault on the Manawan academy comes amid a bloody surge of militant violence across Pakistan and the wider South Asian region. 

Just 27 days prior, on March 3, a group of gunmen launched a strikingly similar ambush on the Sri Lankan cricket team’s bus in downtown Lahore, killing six police officers and injuring several international athletes. That attack effectively ended international sports tours in the country and exposed severe intelligence failures in Punjab province.

Security analysts note that the operational discipline of the Manawan attack strongly resembles the November 2008 Mumbai attacks, in which a small group of heavily armed gunmen held India's financial capital hostage for three days, leaving 166 people dead. 

Furthermore, Pakistan’s urban centers have suffered a string of devastating bombings over the past six months, including the September 2008 truck bombing of the Marriott Hotel in Islamabad, which killed 54 people.

The incident also arrives at a politically sensitive moment for Islamabad. Just days ago, U.S. President Barack Obama announced a new strategy for the region, placing Pakistan at the center of the fight against al-Qaeda and the Taliban, and pledging increased civilian aid alongside stricter accountability for counterterrorism efforts.

As night fell in Lahore, security was placed on high alert across all major Pakistani cities, with extra checkpoints erected along the capital’s diplomatic enclave and security surrounding military and police installations severely heightened.

**By CNN Staff**
Updated 4:15 AM EDT, Tuesday, October 24, 2023

**PESHAWAR, Pakistan (CNN) —** Pakistani security forces have ended an eight-hour siege at a police headquarters in the northwestern city of Peshawar, killing all barricaded militants and rescuing trapped personnel following a violent overnight battle, senior law enforcement officials told CNN on Tuesday. 

At least four police officers and two civilians were killed during the coordinated assault, while another 14 people sustained injuries, according to officials at the nearby Lady Reading Hospital. All five attackers involved in the complex siege were neutralized by elite counter-terrorism commandos.

The attack began around 11:00 p.m. local time on Monday, when heavily armed assailants detonated a vehicle-borne explosive device at the main gate of the district police compound before storming the administrative block. The attackers—equipped with suicide vests, automatic assault rifles, and rocket-propelled grenades—fortified themselves on the top floor of the building, taking several night-shift staff members hostage.

"It was a highly tactical, complex operation. The terrorists were heavily armed and prepared for a prolonged fight," said Senior Superintendent of Police Tariq Khan. "Our primary objective was to secure the safe extraction of our trapped personnel while systematically clearing the compound room by room."

Special forces units from the army's Special Service Group (SSG) and local counter-terrorism police were deployed to the scene shortly after midnight, surrounding the complex. 

Throughout the night, heavy gunfire and periodic explosions echoed across the city as military snipers engaged the militants. Power to the immediate area was cut off to give assault teams a tactical advantage under the cover of darkness.

By 7:00 a.m. local time, authorities confirmed that the final barricaded militant had detonated his suicide vest after being wounded by commando fire, signaling the end of the operation. Bomb disposal units were immediately dispatched to sweep the facility for unexploded ordnance and booby traps.

While no militant group has officially claimed responsibility for the assault, suspicion immediately fell on Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), also known as the Pakistani Taliban. The outlawed group has dramatically escalated its campaign of violence against law enforcement across Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province over the past year, frequently targeting police stations and checkpoints.

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif condemned the assault in a statement released early Tuesday morning, praising the swift response of the security forces.

"The entire nation stands united behind our brave police and armed forces, who laid down their lives to defeat these forces of terror," Sharif said. "Our resolve to eradicate terrorism from Pakistani soil remains unshakable."

**LAHORE, Pakistan** — Heavy gunfire and explosions echoed across eastern Pakistan today as elite security forces stormed the Manawan Police Academy, ending an eight-hour siege by heavily armed gunmen who had infiltrated the facility, taken dozens of hostages, and thrown the country’s second-largest city into chaos.

At least eight police recruits and a civilian were killed, and more than 90 people were injured in the audacious, morning attack on the outskirts of Lahore, located just miles from the Indian border. 

The siege ended late Monday afternoon after Pakistani commandos, paramilitary Rangers, and police launched a dramatic counter-offensive, swarming the compound, neutralizing several attackers, and capturing at least three suspects alive.

### The Attack and Hostage Crisis

The violence began around 7:30 a.m. local time when a group of 10 to 12 militants, armed with assault rifles, hand grenades, and suicide vests, scaled the rear walls and forced their way through the front gates of the training facility. 

Eyewitnesses reported that the attackers threw grenades into a parade ground where roughly 700 unarmed recruits were conducting morning drills. Chaos ensued as terrified cadets rushed for cover under a hail of automatic gunfire.

"We were standing in formation when we heard loud explosions near the gate," said one surviving recruit, receiving treatment for shrapnel wounds at a local hospital. "Militants clad in civilian clothes began firing indiscriminately. They took over the main administrative building and pushed us up to the upper floors, using us as human shields."

For hours, the gunmen held dozens of recruits hostage inside the main building, positioning snipers on the academy's rooftop to hold off arriving security personnel. 

### The Security Forces' Raid

As the standoff intensified, Pakistani authorities deployed army commandos from the Special Service Group (SSG) alongside paramilitary Rangers. Helicopter gunships hovered above, providing aerial surveillance as armored vehicles breached the academy’s perimeter.

In a meticulously coordinated assault, security forces launched a floor-by-floor raid to clear the facility. Smoke billowed from the compound as heavy gun battles broke out inside the corridors. Commandos used tear gas and flashbangs to disorient the militants while systematically freeing trapped recruits.

By mid-afternoon, elite troops had secured the rooftop, firing downward at remaining pockets of resistance. TV broadcast footage showed troops on the roof raising their weapons in victory, signaling the end of the operation.

Internal Security Minister Rehman Malik confirmed that four terrorists were killed by security forces, three were arrested, and at least two detonated their explosive vests to avoid capture.

### Baitullah Mehsud Suspected

Pakistani intelligence officials quickly pointed the finger at the Pakistani Taliban (Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP), specifically pointing to top commander **Baitullah Mehsud**, operating out of the lawless Waziristan tribal region along the Afghan border.

Hours after the compound was secured, Mehsud called several news outlets to claim responsibility for the assault. Speaking to media by telephone from an undisclosed location, Mehsud declared that the attack was launched in retaliation for ongoing U.S. drone strikes against militant hideouts in South Waziristan and Pakistani military operations in the region.

"We accept responsibility for this attack," Mehsud said, threatening further strikes against government targets unless military operations in the tribal regions were halted.

Interior Minister Malik affirmed that initial investigations strongly suggest the hand of Mehsud’s network, calling the attack a direct assault on the Pakistani state. 

"The perpetrators came from the tribal area, and the footprints lead directly to Waziristan," Malik told reporters in Islamabad. "Baitullah Mehsud is attempting to destabilize the nation, but the state will respond with full force."

### Broader Context and Aftermath

The raid at the Manawan academy comes just weeks after a high-profile attack on the Sri Lankan cricket team in downtown Lahore, raising grave concerns about the growing reach of militant networks deep into Punjab, Pakistan's most populous province, far from the traditional combat zones along the Afghan border.

Government buildings, police stations, and military installations across the country have been placed on maximum alert following today’s attack. World leaders have condemned the siege, expressing solidarity with Pakistan as it struggles against a rising wave of domestic terrorism. 

As forensics teams sweep the ruined academy complex for evidence and unexploded ordnance, the Pakistani government faces renewed pressure to bolster domestic intelligence and mount a decisive response against Mehsud’s strongholds in the northwest.

**Militants Storm Lahore Police Academy in Deadly Eight-Hour Siege**

**LAHORE, Pakistan — March 30, 2009** — Heavily armed militants stormed a prominent police training academy on the outskirts of Lahore on Monday morning, launching a commando-style assault that sparked an eight-hour siege and left at least eight police recruits dead and more than 90 injured. 

The siege at the Manawan Police Academy is the second major terrorist attack to strike Pakistan’s eastern cultural capital in less than a month, highlighting a alarming shift in militant tactics and the expanding reach of extremist networks into the country’s heartland.

The attack began around 7:30 a.m. local time when as many as ten gunmen, disguised in police uniforms and carrying backpacks filled with explosives and automatic weapons, scaled the academy walls and lobbed grenades into an open field where hundreds of unarmed recruits were conducting morning drills.

"We were standing in formation when suddenly explosions went off and bullets started flying from all directions," said Imran Zaman, an injured recruit recovering at a nearby hospital. "It was total chaos. We had no weapons to fight back."

The militants quickly seized the main administration building, taking several trainees hostage and positioning snipers on the roof. Pakistani elite security forces, backed by armored vehicles and military helicopters, responded rapidly, surrounding the compound and plunging the facility into a protracted firefight that echoed across the city.

The standoff ended late Monday afternoon after Pakistani security forces launched a coordinated final assault. Officials confirmed that at least four militants were killed, while three were captured alive, including one suspect arrested while attempting to flee the scene in civilian clothing. Interior Ministry officials reported that at least one attacker detonated a suicide vest to avoid capture.

Responsibility for the attack was later claimed by Baitullah Mehsud, the leader of the Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), who threatened further violence unless U.S. drone strikes in the border region were halted and Pakistani forces withdrew from the tribal areas.

### A City Under Siege

Monday’s brazen assault has shattered any lingering sense of security in Lahore, a city of over eight million people that had long been spared the violent insurgency plaguing the northwestern border regions near Afghanistan. 

The siege comes just 27 days after a shockingly similar attack targeted the Sri Lankan national cricket team in downtown Lahore on March 3. In that incident, a dozen gunmen ambushed a convoy carrying the foreign athletes near Liberty Square as they traveled to a match at Gaddafi Stadium. Six police officers guarding the team and two civilians were killed, while seven Sri Lankan players and a coach were wounded. 

The March 3 attack effectively brought an end to international sports in Pakistan, prompting the Sri Lankan team to immediately evacuate the country and causing international cricket authorities to strip Pakistan of its co-hosting duties for the 2011 Cricket World Cup.

Security analysts note striking operational similarities between the two March attacks, pointing to sophisticated reconnaissance, commando-style tactics, and heavy weaponry—including rocket-propelled grenades and assault rifles. Both incidents demonstrate a coordinated effort by extremist groups to undermine the Pakistani state and isolate the nation internationally.

### Heightened Alarm in Islamabad

Speaking to reporters in Islamabad following the end of the siege, Pakistan’s Interior Ministry chief, Rehman Malik, called the police academy attack an assault on the nation's sovereignty.

"This is not an isolated incident; our country is facing a full-scale war," Malik said. "The enemy is trying to destabilize Pakistan from within, moving from the border areas into our major cities."

The rapid succession of high-profile attacks in Punjab province has intensified pressure on the Pakistani government and military to confront militant groups operating within the country's interior, beyond the traditional conflict zones of the Federally Administered Tribal Areas (FATA) and Swat Valley. 

As night fell in Lahore, a strict curfew remained in place around the Manawan facility while forensic teams searched the debris for booby traps and evidence. For the residents of Lahore, the second major tragedy in less than four weeks has left the city in a state of mourning and deep anxiety over what may come next.
